Hook: On the twenty-sixth of July 2012, the euro looked as if it might break apart. Spain was paying 6.8 percent to borrow for ten years, Italy 6.0, while Germany paid 1.2. Investors were pricing the chance that a country would leave the currency, or default. That day the president of the European Central Bank, Mario Draghi, told an investment conference in London: within our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough. In September the bank announced the programme behind the sentence: it would buy a country's short-term bonds without limit, on conditions. It never bought a single one.

Here are the yields, month by month. Germany's in grey, and Britain's in blue: Britain is outside the euro and borrows in a currency its own central bank issues. Italy in green and Spain in gold climb away from them from 2010. Then the sentence. Two years later Spain paid 2.7 percent and Italy 2.8, about what Britain paid. Their debts had not shrunk in those two years; they had grown. What changed was a promise by a central bank, which never had to be kept. This part asks how a central bank can do that, and how anyone can tell what it achieves.

This part's question: what does a central bank actually do, and how do we know what it achieves? What it does, day to day, to set an interest rate. How anyone can measure the effects of its decisions, when it makes them because of what it sees coming. And what it can do when its rate is already at zero, or when a country's debt is under attack.
Economics, Built. Part thirty-one: the central bank.

Here is the plan. The central bank's balance sheet, the market for reserves, and how a rate is set there; then you take the chair in 1979. How the rate reaches spending and prices, and why its effects are so hard to measure. Four answers to that problem, each run on the Island, where the true effect is known. Policy rules with the data of the day, and the tools for when the rate is at zero: asset purchases, promises, negative rates. The neutral rate of interest, the euro crisis, the central bank's words as a tool, and three dials.
Balance: Chapter one. The balance sheet: reserves, a corridor and a floor.

Start with a central bank's balance sheet, as a T-account: what it owns on the left, what it owes on the right. It owns government bonds and loans to banks. It owes two kinds of money: currency, and reserves, which are the accounts banks keep with it. A commercial bank holds reserves as an asset, alongside its loans and bonds, and owes its depositors. Reserves are the money banks pay one another with. A bank short of reserves at the end of the day borrows them overnight from one that has spare, and the price of that loan is the overnight rate: in America, the federal funds rate. The central bank can set that price because it alone can create reserves, or take them away.

Here is the market for reserves. The blue curve is banks' demand: the scarcer reserves are, the more a bank will pay to borrow them overnight. The central bank pays interest on reserves, here one percent, so no bank lends them for less: that is a floor. And it lends to any sound bank against collateral at three percent, so no bank pays more: a ceiling. Before 2008 the Federal Reserve kept reserves scarce, in the steep part of the curve, and set the rate within the corridor by adding or draining small amounts every morning. Add ten units, and the rate falls from 2 percent to 1.50.

Now flood the system with reserves. On the flat part of the curve, banks have more than they need, and the overnight rate sits on the floor, the rate the central bank pays on reserves. Take a sixth of the reserves away, and nothing happens to the rate. To raise the rate, the central bank simply raises what it pays on reserves, and the market rate rises with it. In a floor system the quantity of reserves and the interest rate come apart. The rate is set by an announcement; the size of the balance sheet becomes a second, separate tool.

This is what America did. Before the crisis the Federal Reserve's assets were about 0.9 trillion dollars, and banks' reserves were tiny: about 10 billion dollars in August 2008. In October 2008 the Fed began paying interest on reserves, and then bought bonds on an enormous scale. Reserves peaked at 4.2 trillion dollars in 2021. On the right, the federal funds rate, and the rate paid on reserves in dashes. Since 2008 the market rate has followed the administered rate, a little below it: the Federal Reserve moved from a corridor to a floor, and in 2019 said it would stay there.
PlayIt: Chapter two. Play it: the chair in 1979.

Your turn in the chair. It is early 1979, and this is what is on your desk. Consumer prices rose 8.9 percent over 1978. Since 1947, American output has grown about 3.5 percent a year on average. And by the figures published that winter, output at the end of 1978 was 1.5 percent below that trend: room to grow, it seems, without pushing prices up. The federal funds rate is 10 percent. These are the numbers as they were published at the time, from an archive the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia keeps of every release.

Now the question. With everything learned and revised since, the Congressional Budget Office estimates what the economy could have produced in each quarter without speeding up inflation: its potential. Where does today's estimate put output at the end of 1978? About four percent below potential, so even more room than you thought; about at potential; or about two percent above it? Pause, and choose.

Today's estimate: output was 2.3 percent from its potential, above it, not below. If you chose C, you knew something nobody knew in 1979. The trend of the fifties and sixties had ended: productivity growth slowed after 1973, and estimates made by extending the old trend saw slack that was not there. Put the two gaps into Taylor's rule from Part 30. With the data of the day it says 13.7 percent; with today's, 15.6. The actual rate was 10, below both. Athanasios Orphanides showed that the Federal Reserve's own real-time estimates of the gap in the 1970s were far too optimistic about potential output, and argued that this misreading, rather than a lack of resolve alone, explains much of the Great Inflation. A rule is only as good as the data put into it.
Transmission: Chapter three. Transmission: from one overnight rate to the economy.

A central bank sets one price: the rate on overnight loans between banks. How does that reach a family buying a house, or a firm deciding on a factory? Through several channels at once. Rates on longer loans and bonds move with the overnight rate and with what markets expect it to be. Banks lend less, and least to riskier borrowers. Prices of houses and shares fall, and people who feel poorer spend less. The currency rises, which makes exports dearer abroad. And expectations, of future rates and of inflation, shift at once. All of them end in spending, which moves output and jobs first and prices later. Milton Friedman called the delays long and variable: a year or more before output responds fully, longer for prices. That is why a central bank must act on forecasts, which is the root of everything hard in this part.

The expectations channel can be seen directly. Here is the tightening of 2022. In pink, the top of the federal funds rate's range: zero point two five percent until March 2022, then up to 4.3 by December. In gold, the two-year Treasury yield. It began to climb in the autumn of 2021, from 0.24 percent in September to 1.9 by March, before the Federal Reserve had raised its rate at all. The ten-year yield followed. Markets price the path they expect, so a central bank that is believed moves borrowing costs before it moves its own rate.
Problem: The central question of this part is how anyone can know what a central bank's decisions do. Here is why it is hard. On the Island, the central bank sets its rate each quarter, and output moves. But the bank does not move at random. It sees news before anyone else, about next quarter's demand and next quarter's costs, and acts on it: it raises its rate when it sees a boom coming. Only a small part of each move is the bank's own choice, unrelated to what it sees. That part is the policy shock. On the Island we know exactly what it is, because we planted it.

Now be an economist on the Island who sees only the data. Each dot is a quarter: the change in the policy rate, and output the quarter after. The fitted line slopes up: a one-point rise in the rate goes with output 1.37 percent higher next quarter. Raising rates, it seems, causes booms. The truth, which we planted, is the opposite: a one-point policy shock lowers output by 0.25 percent the next quarter. The rate rises because the bank saw the boom coming, and the boom arrives anyway. Correlation here measures the bank's foresight, not the effect of its decisions.

The same trap catches real data. Take American monthly data from 1965 to 2007 and fit a vector autoregression: each variable on the past of all of them, with the funds rate ordered last, so that the part of a rate move the recent data cannot explain counts as the shock. After a tightening, prices rise: by 0.34 percent after two years, in red, with a band from two hundred re-runs of the data. Christopher Sims found this in 1992, and Martin Eichenbaum named it the price puzzle. Sims's fix was to add commodity prices, which move early when inflation is coming. In gold: 0.17 percent at two years, and minus 0.43 at four. The puzzle is the identification problem again: the Federal Reserve knew inflation was coming and tightened against it; the econometrician, without that knowledge, blamed the tightening for the inflation.
Methods: Chapter five. Four answers, scored against the truth.

Economists have found four main ways to isolate the part of a rate move that is the bank's own. Recursive VARs, which you just saw: assume the bank reacts to this month's data but the economy does not react to the bank within the month, and call what the data cannot explain a shock. Lawrence Christiano, Martin Eichenbaum and Charles Evans set out the standard version in 1999. Narrative shocks: Christina and David Romer read the Federal Reserve's own forecasts, in the staff's Greenbook, and took as the shock the part of each decision those forecasts cannot explain. High-frequency surprises: futures markets price the expected rate, so the move in futures prices in a narrow window around an announcement is what the market did not expect: a day for Kenneth Kuttner in 2001, half an hour for Mark Gertler and Peter Karadi, who used such surprises as instruments in 2015. And a warning from Emi Nakamura and Jón Steinsson: an announcement also tells markets what the bank knows about the economy, so a surprise is not purely the bank's own choice.

Now run all of them on the Island: 300 histories of 60 years each, about as long as America's postwar record, and average what each method finds. The truth, white and dashed: after a one-point policy shock, output falls by 0.4 percent at the trough, three quarters later, and inflation falls slowly. The naive regression gets even the sign wrong, for both. The recursive VAR does better, but output first rises, and inflation rises 0.44 points: the Island has a price puzzle too, because the bank acts on news the VAR cannot see. Add a noisy proxy for the bank's news about costs, as Sims added commodity prices, and the price puzzle shrinks, but output's response is still wrong at first, because nothing in the VAR proxies for the demand news.

Narrative shocks, in gold. On the Island the bank's forecasts include its news, so the part of each decision they cannot explain is almost exactly the planted shock: the correlation is 0.99. The average response lies on the truth. High-frequency surprises, in green, when the announcement carries no news about the economy: also on the truth. But averages over three hundred histories are a luxury. The shaded band holds ninety percent of what one sixty-year history gives with the narrative method: wide enough to include no effect at all on inflation. America has only one history.

Now suppose that when the bank raises its rate, markets also learn that it sees strong demand ahead, and that the surprise carries, along with the shock, 60 percent of the bank's reaction to its demand news. The clean surprises, in green, as before. The contaminated ones, in red: output seems to rise in the first quarter, and its fall is about half the truth. Inflation's fall is halved as well. A tightening that reveals good news about the economy looks less contractionary than it is. Nakamura and Steinsson found this pattern in American data: after surprise tightenings, forecasters revised up their forecasts of output growth. Separating the bank's choice from the bank's information is still the frontier of this literature.
Consensus: What do the better methods find for America? Here is the recursive VAR with commodity prices, on monthly data from 1965 to 2007, with bands from re-running it on resampled data. Industrial production falls slowly after a one-point tightening, and bottoms out -1.3 percent lower after 29 months. Consumer prices barely move for two years, then begin to fall, and the band includes zero almost throughout. That shape is the consensus, and it is what Part 30's model was given habits and indexation to match: output first, after a year or more; prices later, and less surely.

How big is the effect? A standard recursive VAR on 1969 to 1996 finds that a one-point tightening lowers industrial production by about seven tenths of a percent at the worst. The Romers' narrative shocks, on the same years, find four point three percent, with prices about six percent lower after four years. Olivier Coibion traced most of the gap to the years 1979 to 1982, when the Federal Reserve targeted reserves rather than a rate, and to the number of lags each method allows; reconciled, he put the effect at two to three percent. This film's own VAR gives 1.3. The direction and the delays are settled. The size still varies by a factor of six across careful studies, as Valerie Ramey's survey for the Handbook of Macroeconomics documents.
Realtime: Chapter seven. Rules with the data of the day.

Your Play it was one year. Here are all of them. In green, the output gap at the end of each year as it looked the following winter: a trend fitted to everything that winter's figures contained, and output's distance from it. In teal, today's estimate of the same gap, from the Congressional Budget Office's potential output and today's revised figures. Through the 1970s, the data of the day put output on average 2.4 points further below potential than we now think it was. The trend extended the fast growth of the fifties and sixties, after productivity growth had slowed. And a mechanical trend makes the same mistake after the slowdown of the 2000s. Real forecasters did better than this simple line, but the point stands: the gap a rule needs cannot be seen, only estimated, and the estimates were worst exactly when they mattered most.

What would Taylor's rule have said? The federal funds rate, in pink. The rule with the gap of the day, in green, and with today's gap, dashed. In the 1970s the actual rate was on average 2.9 points below what the rule would have said with the data of the day, and 4.1 points below what it says with today's. On this simple measure, misreading the gap explains about a point of the shortfall. Orphanides went further, with the forecasts and gap estimates the committee actually had in front of it. He found that before 1979, as after, the Federal Reserve responded strongly to its forecasts of inflation; the difference was that it also responded strongly to gaps that later proved far too optimistic. The lessons: respond firmly to inflation, and be humble about the gap.
Zero: Chapter eight. The zero bound in practice.

Part 30's model treated the zero bound as a thought experiment. It became the main problem of central banking for two decades. Japan got there first. After its bubble burst, the Bank of Japan cut its rate to near zero by 1999, and it stayed at or below a tenth of a percent for about 21 of the next 27 years. In 2001 the bank began buying assets to expand its balance sheet, the first quantitative easing. The Federal Reserve reached zero in December 2008, stayed there seven years, and returned in March 2020 for two more. The European Central Bank went further, and in June 2014 set its deposit rate below zero, where it stayed for eight years, reaching -0.5 percent. When the rate cannot fall, a central bank still has its balance sheet and its words. The next two chapters are about what those achieved.
QE: Quantitative easing in T-accounts. The central bank buys a hundred of long-term government bonds from a pension fund, and pays by crediting a hundred of new reserves to the fund's bank, which credits the fund's deposit. The fund now holds a deposit instead of a bond. Nothing has been given away: the private sector holds less long-term debt and more short-term money. In a world without frictions, Neil Wallace showed in 1981, such a swap changes nothing at all, since both are liabilities of the government in the end. In this world, some investors, like pension funds, need long bonds to match long promises, and when the central bank removes some, the rest become dearer: long yields fall. Dimitri Vayanos and Jean-Luc Vila wrote that mechanism down as a model of preferred habitats.

This is what the Federal Reserve did. Its assets were 0.9 trillion dollars in August 2008. Three rounds of purchases between late 2008 and 2014 took them past four trillion; from 2017 they were allowed to run off. In 2020 came the largest round of all, and a peak of 9.0 trillion dollars in 2022. Since then the Fed has let them shrink again, to 6.7 trillion. Did any of it work?

The first test was an event study. Joseph Gagnon, Matthew Raskin, Julie Remache and Brian Sack picked the eight days between November 2008 and November 2009 that brought news about the first purchases, and measured what long yields did on each. Here is the ten-year Treasury yield on those days, from close to close. The announcement of the twenty-fifth of November: -24 basis points. The eighteenth of March 2009, when the Fed said it would buy Treasuries: -51. Together, 94 basis points; their own figure was ninety-one. Their models of the term premium gave a similar range. The sceptics' reply: on all the other days of the period, the same yield rose by 143 basis points, as the economy recovered and deficits grew, and the result depends on which days you pick. Ben Bernanke's verdict, at the Brookings Institution in January 2014, as he left office: the problem with QE is that it works in practice, but it doesn't work in theory.
Tools: Chapter ten. Forward guidance, negative rates, yield-curve control.

At zero, a central bank can still promise. In August 2011 the Federal Reserve said it expected to keep its rate exceptionally low at least through mid-2013: a date. In December 2012 it swapped the date for conditions: at least as long as unemployment stayed above six and a half percent, and projected inflation no more than half a point above its two percent goal. Promises like these move what markets expect the rate to be over the next year or two, so they show up in two-year yields. Eric Swanson separated the two tools on announcement days: guidance moved short and medium-term yields, purchases moved the longest. Both worked in the expected direction. But none of them came close to the enormous power that Part 30's model gives a promise: the forward guidance puzzle, seen from the data's side.

Could the rate go below zero? The European Central Bank tried. From June 2014 it charged banks for holding reserves, and by 2019 the charge was 0.5 percent a year. The Bank of Japan followed in 2016. The true floor is not zero but the cost of storing cash instead, which is small but not nothing, and rates went a little below zero without a rush into banknotes. The catch was the banks. Few charged ordinary depositors, so the rates banks paid stayed near zero while the rates they earned fell, squeezing the margins that fund their lending: Gauti Eggertsson and coauthors found that in Sweden this blunted the cuts. Negative rates helped a little, and at a cost.

The third tool sets a price instead of a quantity. In September 2016 the Bank of Japan announced that it would hold the ten-year government bond yield around zero, buying whatever it took to do so. It kept the target in some form until March 2024. In March 2020 the Reserve Bank of Australia held the three-year yield at a tenth of a percent. As inflation rose, markets bet against it; the bank ended up owning most of the bond it targeted, and in November 2021 it gave up. A yield target is a promise that markets can test, every day. It holds while it is believed, which is a theme the euro crisis will make vivid in two chapters.
Neutral: Chapter eleven. The neutral rate, estimated.

Part 30 left a question: every rule needs the natural rate of interest, the real rate at which policy neither pushes the economy nor holds it back, and nobody can see it. How is it estimated? On the Island, we can check. Here the natural rate drifts slowly, in white, over fifty years. The bank infers it the way Thomas Laubach and John Williams did for America: if output keeps falling short while the real rate seems low, the natural rate must be lower than thought. The Kalman filter turns that into an estimate, in teal. The band holds ninety percent of the uncertainty: plus or minus 0.8 points, even with the model exactly right. The estimate trails the truth by years, because the natural rate shows itself only through slow drifts in output that other shocks swamp.

Here are the estimates for real economies. The New York Fed publishes Kathryn Holston, Thomas Laubach and John Williams's estimates every quarter. For the United States: about 3.7 percent in 2000, 0.9 percent by 2015, and 1.0 percent in the latest. Canada's and the euro area's fell too; the euro area's to about zero. The gold dots are the Federal Reserve's policymakers' own view of where their rate settles in the long run, less two percent inflation: 2.3 percent in 2012, as low as 0.4, and 1.2 now. The causes most often given are slower growth, ageing populations that save more, and a world hungry for safe assets. Whatever the cause, a lower natural rate means the zero bound is hit more often, which is why the tools of the last three chapters will be needed again.
Euro: Chapter twelve. The euro and the lender of last resort.

Why could a sentence lower Spain's borrowing costs? Because the crisis was partly self-fulfilling. Take a government that owes a hundred and twenty percent of its income, and will default if the interest bill grows larger than the taxes it can raise, an amount nobody knows exactly. Investors who expect a higher yield expect a bigger bill, so a higher chance of default, so they demand a higher yield still: the purple curve. Where the curve meets the diagonal, expectations are fulfilled. At 2.5 percent, the bill is small, default is unlikely, and the low yield is justified. At 6 percent, the bill is large, default likely, and the high yield justified too. Expect a little more, and yields spiral up until no one will lend at all. The country's debts are the same in both. Which equilibrium it gets depends on what investors expect, which was Guillermo Calvo's point in 1988 and Paul De Grauwe's about the euro area in 2011.

Now add a lender of last resort. The central bank promises to buy the country's bonds, without limit, at 3.5 percent. The bill can no longer grow with investors' fears, so neither can the chance of default: the curve goes flat. The bad equilibrium is gone; only the good one is left. Start from a panic, and yields now run back down. And if investors believe the promise, nobody sells at the bad price, so the central bank never has to buy. This is Part 26's bank run again, with a country in place of a bank, and deposit insurance in the form of a sentence. Walter Bagehot's rule from 1873 was to lend freely, against good collateral, to solvent borrowers; Draghi's conditions were the modern version of good collateral.

Why were Spain and Italy exposed, and not Britain? In 2011 Britain's public debt was eighty-five percent of its GDP, Spain's sixty-nine. Yet Britain paid barely more than Germany to borrow, while Spain paid 5.6 points more by July 2012, and Italy 4.8. De Grauwe's explanation: Britain borrows in pounds, and the Bank of England can always create pounds, so a run on British debt cannot end in a default forced by a lack of cash. Spain and Italy borrowed in euros that neither could create, so investors could force them into the bad equilibrium. Draghi's sentence gave the euro area what Britain had: a central bank that would stand behind its governments' debts, within its mandate.
Words: For most of its history the Federal Reserve said as little as possible. Until 1994 it did not even announce its decisions: markets inferred them from its trading. In February 1994 it issued its first statement after a meeting. In April 2011 the chair held the first regular press conference. In January 2012 it adopted a numerical goal of two percent inflation, and began publishing each policymaker's projection of the rate, the dots. In December 2012 it tied its guidance to unemployment. The reason is the theory of the last two parts: if expectations do much of the work, then shaping them is the policy, and a central bank that is understood needs to move its rate less.

Words move prices, sometimes more than intended. On the twenty-second of May 2013, Ben Bernanke told Congress that the Fed might slow its bond purchases in the next few meetings, if the economy kept improving. The ten-year yield had been 1.94 percent the day before. By the end of the year it was 3.04 percent, 110 basis points higher: the taper tantrum. The Fed did not decide to slow its purchases until December. A sentence about the future had tightened financial conditions without any change in policy at all: the expectations channel, working in a direction the speaker had not intended.
Practice: Chapter fifteen. In practice: policy staff and rates strategists.

Who does this work? Inside a central bank, staff economists run the forecast round. Before every meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee they produce a complete forecast, once called the Greenbook for its cover and now the Tealbook. They add alternative scenarios, the prescriptions of several rules with the data of the day, and simulations with models like Part 30's. Outside, on the trading floors of banks and funds, rates strategists compare the path of rates that markets price with the path the central bank signals, and read every statement for each changed word. Both sides use the tools of this part: shocks and their effects, real-time data, and an estimate of the neutral rate that nobody trusts very far.

And a claim about the staff's forecasts. Called it? In 2000, Christina and David Romer showed that the Federal Reserve's own staff forecast inflation better than commercial forecasters: once you knew the Greenbook, the others told you almost nothing. That is why, they argued, markets learn from the Fed's moves. The Greenbooks are released after five years, so the claim can be checked out of sample. Over the four quarters ahead, from 1969 to 1991, the staff's typical error was 1.33 points against the professional forecasters' 1.69. From 1992 to 2020 it was 0.98 against 0.95: the edge had gone, perhaps because the Fed began to say so much more. Partly right: true when they wrote it, of the years they studied, and not since.
Frontier: Chapter sixteen. Frontier: after the surge.

The newest test of everything in this part began in 2021. Consumer price inflation rose to 9.0 percent by mid-2022. The Federal Reserve raised its rate from zero to 5.5 percent in sixteen months, the fastest rise since the early 1980s. It started late, about a year after inflation took off, partly because a new framework had promised to let inflation run a little above target after years below it, and partly because the surge was first read as passing. Inflation then fell a long way without the recession many forecasters expected, which the anchored expectations of Part 28 and the supply shocks of Part 30 help explain, and which the profession is still arguing about.

Two consequences are still unwinding. A floor system means paying interest on trillions of reserves. When the Fed raised its rate, it paid more on reserves than it earned on the bonds it had bought at low yields, and from September 2022 it ran losses. It records them as a deferred asset, an amount it will keep back from future payments to the Treasury; at its deepest, in 2026, 246 billion dollars. And it shrank its balance sheet, from 9.0 trillion dollars to 6.7. A central bank can lose money without running out of it, since it creates the money it pays with. Whether losses threaten its independence, and how small the balance sheet can get while reserves stay ample, are open questions.

The open questions. How to separate what a central bank chooses from what its choices reveal. Why the neutral rate fell, and whether it is rising again. How large a balance sheet a floor system needs. How much of the fall in inflation after 2022 was policy, and how much was supply shocks undoing themselves. And how monetary policy reaches households that differ in wealth and debts, which Part 52 takes up.
